q: Where does Lactococcus lactis LL16 sit in the global L. lactis subsp. lactis vs subsp. cremoris phylogeography, and does its indigenous Lithuanian dairy origin leave detectable niche-adaptation signatures (e.g., loss of plant-associated genes, gain of dairy-associated lactose/citrate utilisation loci, prophage flux) that distinguish it from plant-origin L. lactis lineages?
basis: The paper characterises LL16 as an indigenous Lithuanian raw-milk isolate and this replication confirmed same-subspecies status vs UC06 at mash 0.0040 (ANI ~99.6%). That places LL16 firmly in the subsp. lactis clade but leaves entirely open where it falls in the >100-genome global L. lactis pan-phylogeny and whether it carries dairy-niche-adaptation markers (lac operon on plasmid vs chromosome, cit permease, opp-pep proteolytic system amplification, IS-driven pseudogenisation of plant-metabolism genes documented by Kelleher et al., Wels et al.).
next_steps: Pull all L. lactis GenBank complete + draft genomes (~800+), build a core-genome SNP tree (Parsnp/IQ-TREE), place LL16 on it, colour tips by isolation source (raw-milk vs cheese-starter vs plant vs invertebrate), then run Roary/Panaroo to identify dairy-vs-plant accessory-gene presence/absence and check LL16's accessory profile against the dairy-adapted signature. Cross-check against Kelleher 2017 and Wels 2019 markers.

q: What is the complete bacteriocin / nisin / EPS / aroma-compound biosynthesis gene inventory of LL16, and which of those loci are the strongest industrial starter-culture selection markers compared to reference dairy starters (IL1403, MG1363, UC06, SK11)?
basis: The paper reports LcnB (lactococcin B) + EnlA (enterolysin A) bacteriocin clusters and this replication verified both by tblastn on JARHUB010000163.1 and JARHUB010000109.1. The paper also flagged a T3PKS BGC (antiSMASH 5.0) which this replication could only spot-check. Broader industrially relevant traits (nisin A/Z, lactococcin A/M, diacetyl/acetoin from citrate, EPS clusters, aroma esterases) were not systematically enumerated in either the paper or this replication.
next_steps: Run a complete BAGEL4 + antiSMASH 8.x (with full DBs on uicgpu) sweep on LL16, then tblastn a curated panel of industrial-starter markers (nisA/B/T/C/I/P, lacABCDEFG operon, citP, aldB, ilvBN, EPS eps cluster, esterases estA/estB, PepN/PepX proteolysis) against LL16 and against IL1403/MG1363/UC06/SK11 as references. Report LL16's inventory as a scorecard vs a canonical starter-selection rubric.

q: Does LL16's genome-based safety profile (no acquired AMR, no virulence, no biogenic-amine decarboxylases) meet current EFSA QPS / FDA GRAS requirements for use as a starter/adjunct culture and as a probiotic co-culture, and are there any borderline calls (e.g., intrinsic lmrC/lmrD efflux, prophage-carried toxins, mobilisable resistance on the pCI2000-like plasmid) that would need explicit regulatory justification?
basis: This replication confirmed 0 acquired AMR hits (ResFinder/NCBI-betalactamase/ARG-ANNOT at >=90% id / >=60% cov), 0 VFDB virulence hits, and 0 biogenic-amine decarboxylase hits, but also flagged 2 intrinsic Lactococcus efflux genes (lmrC 99.59%, lmrD 99.80%) and did not audit the 372-contig draft for prophage-carried virulence or plasmid-borne mobilisable resistance.
next_steps: Run PHASTER/Phigaro/geNomad for prophage detection on LL16 assembly, then intersect prophage regions with VFDB/toxin HMMs. Run MobileElementFinder + oriTfinder on the pCI2000-like plasmid to check mobilisability. Compare the full LL16 safety scorecard against the EFSA QPS 2023 qualifications list for L. lactis and prepare a QPS-compliance table with any exception justifications.

q: What is the plasmidome content of LL16 beyond the single pCI2000-like repUS4 replicon, and how much of the dairy-fermentation phenotype (lactose/citrate/protease/bacteriocin/EPS) is plasmid-encoded versus chromosomally encoded in LL16?
basis: The paper reports 1 plasmid (repUS4, pCI2000-like at 99.57% id to AF178424) and this replication confirmed pCI2000 hits at 90-99.7% id, longest 1865 bp @ 96.1%. However the 372-contig Illumina draft cannot cleanly resolve whether additional small/cryptic plasmids exist, nor which of the dairy-phenotype loci sit on the plasmid vs the chromosome (a classic L. lactis dairy-strain question: lac and prt are famously plasmid-borne in many strains, e.g. SK11 on pSK11L).
next_steps: Long-read (Nanopore/PacBio) resequencing of LL16 to close the genome into chromosome + plasmid(s), then map every dairy-phenotype gene (lacABCDEFG, prtP/prtM, citP, bacteriocin, EPS eps) to chromosome vs plasmid. Alternatively, from the existing draft, use plasmidSPAdes + PlasFlow + geNomad to identify additional plasmid contigs and BLAST-cluster them against a curated Lactococcus plasmid reference set.

q: How does LL16's prophage-resistance / CRISPR-Cas locus diversity compare to other industrial L. lactis starter cultures, and does its single-array / Cas2-positive CRISPR system (plus native abortive-infection / restriction-modification gene set) provide meaningful protection against the dominant lactococcal phage groups (936, c2, P335) that cause fermentation failures?
basis: The paper reports 1 CRISPR array (3 spacers, DR=23 bp) with an associated Cas gene, and this replication confirmed 1 Cas2 annotation (MDH8063313.1) qualitatively but did not enumerate spacers, classify the CRISPR-Cas system subtype, spacer-match against lactococcal phage genomes, or inventory Abi/RM phage-defence systems. Phage-resistance is the #1 industrial starter-selection criterion after safety.
next_steps: Run CRISPRCasTyper on LL16 to classify the CRISPR-Cas subtype (likely II-A given single Cas2 + short DR), extract all spacers with CRISPRDetect/CRISPRFinder, then BLAST spacers against the NCBI Caudovirales / lactococcal phage genome set (936, c2, P335 group representatives). Additionally run DefenseFinder / PADLOC on LL16 to inventory Abi (AbiA-AbiZ), RM Types I/II/III, and other phage-defence loci, then compare the full defence-system scorecard against SK11/MG1363/IL1403/UC06.
